It is caused by Bundibugyo virus (BDBV), for which no licensed vaccine or therapeutic exists. As of 11 August 2026, the national response had reported 4,566 confirmed cases and 2,128 confirmed deaths, corresponding to a case/fatality ratio of 46.6%. During the preceding 24 h alone, 118 new confirmed cases and 67 deaths were reported — the highest daily number of confirmed cases recorded during the outbreak1. This trajectory continues despite substantial surveillance. Of 324 suspected cases validated during the reporting period, 99.7% were investigated, while 17,085 out of 20,728 contacts were followed, giving a national follow-up coverage of 82.4%. These figures demonstrate operational capacity, but they also expose a fundamental limitation of conventional outbreak dashboards: coverage is not the same as effectiveness. The proportion of alerts investigated, or contacts followed, describes the reach of surveillance; it does not establish whether surveillance was sufficiently timely to prevent secondary transmission1. This distinction matters for BDBV. Unlike Zaire ebolavirus, for which licensed vaccines and therapeutics exist, no vaccine or specific therapeutic is available for BDBV. Consequently, rapid detection, isolation, infection prevention and control, supportive care and community engagement remain central to outbreak control2,3,4. The humanitarian and health-system context of this outbreak pose additional challenges2,3. The crucial unit of performance should be the interval between detection and intervention. Surveillance is valuable only if alerts can be rapidly translated into investigation, laboratory confirmation, isolation, appropriate care, contact tracing, and sustained follow-up. These steps form a temporal chain in which delay at any point creates opportunities for onward transmission. Evidence from previous Ebola outbreaks supports this interpretation: delayed isolation has been associated with community transmission, while modeling studies indicate that shortening time to isolation can substantially reduce epidemic size, even when diagnostic sensitivity is not optimal5,6. The DRC outbreak provides an unusually clear signal of this problem. Ituri accounted for 3,912 of the 4,566 confirmed cases and 98 of the 118 new cases reported during the preceding 24 h. Of its 36 health zones, 28 were affected. At the same time, the response reported important constraints: two ambulances were out of service in Ituri, seven health zones in North Kivu had no ambulance coverage, four health zones lacked a treatment or isolation center, and several treatment centers were saturated. These constraints create a pathway through which a detected infection may remain transmissible in the community1. Community mortality may be the clearest indicator of this response gap. Of the 67 confirmed deaths reported during the latest 24-h period, 50 occurred in the community and 17 in treatment centers. Community deaths should not be interpreted simply as a downstream measure of disease severity. In an Ebola outbreak, they can also signal that the response pathway failed to reach an infectious individual before death. They may reflect delays in symptom recognition, care seeking, referral, transport, diagnosis or isolation, as well as incomplete contact tracing, inadequate access to care, insecurity or community resistance1. This interpretation is supported by experience from previous Ebola responses. During the 2018–2020 DRC outbreak, delays in isolation and community deaths were recognized as mechanisms that could amplify transmission. In Uganda’s 2022 Sudan virus disease outbreak, 43% of confirmed patients entered effective isolation at least 6 days after symptom onset, with lack of transport and fear of Ebola treatment units as contributors to delayed care7. The relevance of these findings to the present BDBV outbreak is not that the circumstances are identical, but that time outside effective isolation remains a modifiable determinant of both transmission and survival. A recent mathematical modeling study found that shortening time to isolation or increasing testing access could markedly reduce epidemic size, supporting the value of rapid diagnostic-to-isolation pathways6. Meanwhile, genomics has identified a previously unrecorded BDBV variant associated with the current outbreak, reinforcing the importance of combining genomic, epidemiological and operational intelligence rather than relying on case counts alone7. The implication is not that surveillance has failed. Instead, the outbreak suggests that surveillance performance and response performance are partially decoupled. This distinction affects how outbreak response is measured. We propose that Ebola response dashboards add a new response-effectiveness cascade to existing surveillance indicators, measuring, in real time: (i) time from alert to investigation; (ii) time from investigation to specimen collection; (iii) time from specimen collection to laboratory result; (iv) time from confirmation to effective isolation; (v) time from isolation to definitive supportive care; (vi) the proportion of contacts reached within the first follow-up interval; and (vii) the proportion of deaths occurring in the community before effective isolation (Table 1). These indicators would transform surveillance from a system that primarily describes where transmission is occurring into one that also identifies where intervention is failing to occur rapidly enough. Together, they shift the unit of performance from coverage to speed. Importantly, these measures should be disaggregated by health zone. The national contact-follow-up rate of 82.4% approaches the operational threshold of 85%, but this aggregate conceals major heterogeneity: coverage was only 60.7% in North Kivu. National averages can create a false impression of system-wide resilience. The response system is only as strong as its least responsive transmission corridor1. This perspective also reframes community deaths. Instead of treating them solely as an endpoint, response teams could interpret the proportion of deaths that occur outside treatment centers as a sentinel indicator of missed opportunities for intervention. A sudden increase in community deaths should trigger an operational investigation: where were these patients first symptomatic? Were they previously listed as contacts? How long did they remain in the community after symptom onset? Was transport available? Was testing accessible? How long did confirmation take? Were treatment and isolation facilities functioning? Were social, security or trust-related barriers involved? Such questions would connect epidemiological surveillance to the operational reality of outbreak response. They would also complement recent efforts to develop real-time epidemic intelligence for the BDBV outbreak3, with the objective of identifying the bottleneck(s) at which information fails to become action. The central lesson is broader than Ebola. Detection is an information outcome; interruption is a public-health outcome. They should not be measured as if they were equivalent. In an outbreak in which therapeutic and vaccine options remain limited, the interval between these two outcomes will largely determine transmission and mortality. For DRC, and future outbreaks, the ultimate test of surveillance should not be the number of alerts investigated or contacts followed. The ultimate measure of surveillance is how many cases, and deaths, we prevent. analysis.research_question_and_background: The study addresses the challenge of controlling Ebola outbreaks by highlighting the gap between detecting transmission and effectively stopping it, particularly in the context of the Bundibugyo virus (BDBV) outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC).
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study is a retrospective analysis of the DRC's seventeenth Ebola outbreak, focusing on the operational capacity and limitations of surveillance efforts during the period from August 2026. It includes data on confirmed cases, deaths, and contact tracing activities across the country.
analysis.methods: The methods involve reviewing outbreak data, including confirmed cases, deaths, and contact tracing metrics, to evaluate the effectiveness of surveillance and response measures. The study also references previous research and modeling studies to contextualize the findings.
analysis.main_results: As of 11 August 2026, the DRC outbreak had reported 4,566 confirmed cases and 2,128 confirmed deaths, with a case/fatality ratio of 46.6%. During the preceding 24 hours, 118 new confirmed cases and 67 deaths were reported, representing the highest daily number of confirmed cases recorded during the outbreak.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret that high surveillance coverage does not equate to effective outbreak control, emphasizing the need for rapid translation of alerts into action to prevent secondary transmission. This highlights the importance of the response interval as a critical performance metric.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings underscore the necessity of improving the timeliness of outbreak response measures, particularly for BDBV, where no licensed vaccine or therapeutic exists. This has direct implications for surveillance, diagnosis, and community engagement strategies.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its reliance on reported outbreak data and does not provide direct causal evidence of the effectiveness of response measures. The evidence is moderate, as it is based on observational data and references to prior studies.

analysis.summary_en: This study examines the seventeenth Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), emphasizing the critical need to shorten the interval between detection and intervention. Despite high surveillance coverage, the outbreak continued with a high case/fatality ratio and significant daily case numbers, highlighting the limitations of conventional outbreak dashboards. The authors argue that rapid translation of alerts into action is essential to prevent secondary transmission, especially for Bundibugyo virus (BDBV), which lacks a licensed vaccine or therapeutic. The study's findings suggest that improving the timeliness of response measures could enhance outbreak control. However, the evidence is moderate due to reliance on observational data and prior studies, without direct causal analysis of the effectiveness of interventions.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究探讨了控制埃博拉暴发的挑战,特别强调了在刚果民主共和国(DRC)Bundibugyo病毒(BDBV)暴发背景下,检测传播与有效阻止之间的差距。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 本研究是对刚果民主共和国第十七次埃博拉暴发的回顾性分析,重点考察了2026年8月期间监测行动的能力和局限性。研究包括了全国范围内的确诊病例、死亡病例和接触者追踪数据。
elements_zh.methods: 研究方法包括审查暴发数据,包括确诊病例、死亡病例和接触者追踪指标,以评估监测和响应措施的有效性。研究还参考了先前的研究和建模研究,以提供背景信息。
elements_zh.main_results: 截至2026年8月11日,刚果民主共和国的暴发报告了4,566例确诊病例和2,128例死亡病例,病例/死亡比率为46.6%。在之前的24小时内,报告了118例新确诊病例和67例死亡病例,这是暴发期间记录的最高单日确诊病例数。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者认为,尽管监测覆盖率很高,但这并不等同于有效的暴发控制,强调了将警报迅速转化为行动的必要性,以防止继发性传播。这突显了响应时间作为关键绩效指标的重要性。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现强调了提高暴发响应措施及时性的必要性,特别是在BDBV的情况下,目前尚无批准的疫苗或治疗方法。这对监测、诊断和社区参与策略有直接的影响。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究受限于其依赖于报告的暴发数据,并未提供响应措施有效性的直接因果证据。由于其基于观察数据和先前研究的参考,证据强度中等。

papers.title: Cytokine-induced nuclear translocation of STAT1 via a non-transferable NLS
papers.abstract: The targeting function of nuclear localization signals (NLSs) is generally considered independent of a protein's native sequence or fold and is readily transferable to heterologous cargos. Contrary to this paradigm, rapid nuclear translocation of phosphorylated STAT1 (pSTAT1) following cytokine stimulation requires importin {beta}, Ran-GTP, and the importin 5 isoform, which recognizes a non-transferable NLS. Here, we present cryo-EM structures of pSTAT1 bound to importin 5, revealing an asymmetric 2:1 complex that diverges from canonical NLS-mediated cargo recognition. Importin 5 occupies the DNA-binding groove of the pSTAT1 dimer, with a single STAT1 N-terminal domain positioning the C-terminal Armadillo repeats 9-10 (S1B domain) orthogonal to the DNA-binding interface. This interface is also targeted by the Ebola virus protein VP24, an antagonist of interferon signaling. We further show that Ran-GTP alone is insufficient to trigger nuclear release of pSTAT1, which additionally requires the exportin CAS. A cryo-EM reconstruction of the CAS-Ran-GTP-5 complex, supported by in vitro competition assays, demonstrates that CAS and pSTAT1 are mutually exclusive ligands for importin 5. Together, these findings define the molecular choreography of cytokine-induced STAT1 nuclear translocation and release, establishing a general paradigm for STAT family signaling.

analysis.study_design_and_population: The study involved cryo-EM structural analysis of pSTAT1 bound to importin 5, with the investigation centered on the molecular mechanisms of cytokine-induced nuclear translocation and release of pSTAT1.
analysis.methods: The researchers used cryo-EM to reconstruct the structure of pSTAT1-importin 5 complexes and conducted in vitro competition assays to demonstrate the interaction dynamics between CAS, Ran-GTP, and importin 5.
analysis.main_results: The cryo-EM structures revealed an asymmetric 2:1 complex of pSTAT1 and importin 5, and in vitro assays showed that Ran-GTP alone is insufficient for nuclear release, requiring the exportin CAS.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings establish a new paradigm for cytokine-induced STAT1 nuclear translocation, highlighting the non-transferable nature of the NLS and the involvement of importin 5 in a unique molecular interaction.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These results provide insights into the molecular mechanisms of interferon signaling, which could inform the development of targeted therapies for viral infections like Ebola virus disease.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited to structural and in vitro analyses, which may not fully capture in vivo dynamics, but the evidence is strong due to the detailed molecular characterization and experimental validation.

analysis.summary_en: This study challenges the general assumption that nuclear localization signals (NLSs) are transferable to heterologous cargos by demonstrating that cytokine-induced nuclear translocation of phosphorylated STAT1 (pSTAT1) requires a non-transferable NLS recognized by importin 5. Using cryo-EM, the researchers revealed an asymmetric 2:1 complex of pSTAT1 and importin 5, showing that Ran-GTP alone is insufficient for nuclear release, which also necessitates the exportin CAS. The findings establish a new paradigm for cytokine-induced STAT1 nuclear translocation, highlighting the unique molecular interaction involving importin 5. These results provide insights into interferon signaling mechanisms, which could inform the development of targeted therapies for viral infections like Ebola virus disease. However, the study is limited to structural and in vitro analyses, which may not fully capture in vivo dynamics. The evidence is strong due to the detailed molecular characterization and experimental validation.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在挑战核定位信号(NLSs)可以转移到异源货物的一般假设,重点研究细胞因子诱导的磷酸化STAT1(pSTAT1)核转位的特定情况。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 本研究涉及对pSTAT1与importin 5结合的冷冻电镜结构分析,研究重点是细胞因子诱导的pSTAT1核转位和释放的分子机制。
elements_zh.methods: 研究人员使用冷冻电镜重建了pSTAT1-importin 5复合物的结构,并通过体外竞争实验展示了CAS、Ran-GTP与importin 5之间的相互作用动态。
elements_zh.main_results: 冷冻电镜结构揭示了pSTAT1与importin 5形成的非对称2:1复合物,体外实验表明仅Ran-GTP不足以触发核释放,还需要出口蛋白CAS。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 这些发现确立了细胞因子诱导的STAT1核转位的新范式,突出了NLS的不可转移特性以及importin 5在独特分子相互作用中的作用。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些结果为干扰素信号传导的分子机制提供了见解,可能有助于开发针对如埃博拉病毒病等病毒感染的靶向治疗。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 本研究仅限于结构和体外分析,可能无法完全反映体内动态,但由于详细的分子表征和实验验证,其证据是强有力的。

papers.abstract_zh: 核定位信号(NLSs)的靶向功能通常被认为与蛋白质的天然序列或折叠无关,并且可以轻易转移到异源货物上。然而,与这一范式相反,细胞因子刺激后磷酸化STAT1(pSTAT1)的快速核转位需要importin β、Ran-GTP以及识别非可转移NLS的importin 5同种型。在这里,我们展示了pSTAT1与importin 5结合的冷冻电镜结构,揭示了一个与经典NLS介导的货物识别不同的非对称2:1复合物。importin 5占据pSTAT1二聚体的DNA结合沟槽,单个STAT1的N端结构域使C端Armadillo重复序列9-10(S1B结构域)垂直于DNA结合界面。该界面同样被干扰素信号拮抗蛋白埃博拉病毒的VP24所靶向。我们进一步证明,仅Ran-GTP不足以触发pSTAT1的核释放,其还需要出口蛋白CAS。通过冷冻电镜重建的CAS-Ran-GTP-5复合物,结合体外竞争实验,表明CAS和pSTAT1是importin 5的相互排斥配体。这些发现定义了细胞因子诱导的STAT1核转位和释放的分子过程,确立了STAT家族信号传导的一般范式。
papers.summary_zh: 核定位信号(NLSs)的靶向功能通常被认为与蛋白质的天然序列或折叠无关,并且可以轻易转移到异源货物上。然而,与这一范式相反,细胞因子刺激后磷酸化STAT1(pSTAT1)的快速核转位需要importin β、Ran-GTP以及识别非可转移NLS的importin 5同种型。在这里,我们展示了pSTAT1与importin 5结合的冷冻电镜结构,揭示了一个与经典NLS介导的货物识别不同的非对称2:1复合物。importin 5占据pSTAT1二聚体的DNA结合沟槽,单个STAT1的N端结构域使C端Armadillo重复序列9-10(S1B结构域)垂直于DNA结合界面。该界面同样被干扰素信号拮抗蛋白埃博拉病毒的VP24所靶向。我们进一步证明,仅Ran-GTP不足以触发pSTAT1的核释放,其还需要出口蛋白CAS。通过冷冻电镜重建的CAS-Ran-GTP-5复合物,结合体外竞争实验,表明CAS和pSTAT1是importin 5的相互排斥配体。这些发现定义了细胞因子诱导的STAT1核转位和释放的分子过程,确立了STAT家族信号传导的一般范式。

analysis_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在挑战核定位信号(NLSs)可以转移到异源货物的一般假设,重点研究细胞因子诱导的磷酸化STAT1(pSTAT1)核转位的特定情况。
analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 本研究涉及对pSTAT1与importin 5结合的冷冻电镜结构分析,研究重点是细胞因子诱导的pSTAT1核转位和释放的分子机制。
analysis_zh.methods: 研究人员使用冷冻电镜重建了pSTAT1-importin 5复合物的结构,并通过体外竞争实验展示了CAS、Ran-GTP与importin 5之间的相互作用动态。
analysis_zh.main_results: 冷冻电镜结构揭示了pSTAT1与importin 5形成的非对称2:1复合物,体外实验表明仅Ran-GTP不足以触发核释放,还需要出口蛋白CAS。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 这些发现确立了细胞因子诱导的STAT1核转位的新范式,突出了NLS的不可转移特性以及importin 5在独特分子相互作用中的作用。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些结果为干扰素信号传导的分子机制提供了见解,可能有助于开发针对如埃博拉病毒病等病毒感染的靶向治疗。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 本研究仅限于结构和体外分析,可能无法完全反映体内动态,但由于详细的分子表征和实验验证,其证据是强有力的。

news.title_zh: 由本迪布焦病毒引起的埃博拉病 - 刚果民主共和国 - 世界卫生组织 (WHO)
news.source_body_en: The World Health Organization (WHO) reported on 25 September 2026 that an outbreak of Ebola disease caused by the Bundibugyo virus is occurring in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The outbreak is confirmed as a public health emergency, and the WHO has issued statements and recommendations to address it. The scale and impact of the outbreak are not explicitly quantified in the supplied evidence, but it is associated with the Bundibugyo virus, a human-pathogenic Ebola virus. The response status is under investigation, with ongoing efforts to monitor and manage the outbreak. The WHO has emphasized the importance of preparedness and response strategies to mitigate the risk of further spread.
news.content_zh: 世界卫生组织(WHO)于2026年9月25日报告称,刚果民主共和国正在发生由邦迪布古病毒引起的埃博拉病毒病暴发。该暴发已被确认为公共卫生紧急事件,WHO已发布声明和建议以应对这一情况。在提供的证据中,未明确量化该暴发的规模和影响,但其与邦迪布古病毒有关,而邦迪布古病毒是一种人类致病性病毒。应对状态正在调查中,正在进行监测和管理该暴发的持续努力。WHO强调了准备和应对策略的重要性,以减轻进一步传播的风险。

Search|t Updates Countries Disasters Organizations Topics Jobs Training Informing humanitarians worldwide 24/7 — a service provided by UN OCHA DR Congo + 11 more IOM: Multi-Country Bundibugyo Ebola Virus Disease Outbreak - Situation Report No. 19 (14 - 20 September 2026) Format Situation Report Source IOM Posted 25 Sep 2026 Originally published 25 Sep 2026 Origin View original Attachments Download Report (PDF | 740.27 KB) SITUATION OVERVIEW According to the Ministry of Health of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), as of 20 September 2026, the Bundibugyo Ebola virus disease (BVD) outbreak had resulted in 7,733 confirmed cases, 3,732 deaths and 1,902 recoveries, representing a case fatality rate of 48.3 per cent. Since the beginning of the outbreak, 63 of 167 health zones (37.7%) across seven provinces have reported at least one confirmed case, while 55 health zones across five provinces remain classified as active transmission zones. Although several health zones have reported extended periods without detecting new cases, transmission remains concentrated in eastern DRC. A total of 61 newly confirmed cases were reported in Ituri (34), North Kivu (23) and Haut-Uélé (4), with Ituri and North Kivu accounting for 93.4 per cent of all newly reported cases. The continued concentration of transmission in these areas underscores the need to sustain disease surveillance, response and preparedness capacities within affected provinces, while maintaining readiness in neighbouring countries connected through cross-border mobility corridors. While localized progress has been observed in parts of the response, mortality remains a significant concern. Community deaths continue to account for the majority of newly reported deaths, highlighting ongoing challenges related to early detection, timely referral and access to care. These challenges are particularly relevant in settings affected by displacement, insecurity and population movement, where delays in seeking or accessing care may contribute to continued transmission. news.content_title: Hilleman Laboratories to develop and produce CEPI-backed Bundibugyo ebolavirus vaccine doses for clinical trials
news.content: Hilleman Laboratories to develop and produce CEPI-backed Bundibugyo ebolavirus vaccine doses for clinical trials 30 Jul 2026 • 2 min read Press release was issued by CEPI and Hilleman Labs. OSLO/SINGAPORE — The Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations (CEPI) is collaborating with Hilleman Laboratories, a Singapore-based joint venture of biopharmaceutical company MSD and charitable foundation Wellcome, to advance the development and manufacturing of Bundibugyo ebolavirus vaccine candidate doses for clinical trials using the recombinant vesicular stomatitis virus (rVSV) platform. With up to US$8.5 million in CEPI funding, Hilleman Laboratories will advance development and manufacture clinical supply of the investigational vaccine at the organisation’s vaccine production facility as scientists ramp up efforts to respond to one of the largest Ebola outbreaks on record, which is predominantly affecting the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Assuming early phase trials succeed, the partners are committed to swiftly transferring the vaccine technology to a large-scale vaccine manufacturer to produce additional doses, as needed, for later-stage trials. A further aim of the technology transfer would be to ensure rapid, affordable supply of doses in outbreak-affected countries and low- and middle-income settings if the vaccine is authorised for use. "With Bundibugyo virus cases rising at worrying speed, the epidemic is fast becoming a humanitarian crisis. No vaccine is currently approved against the virus, so we are urgently advancing vaccine candidates into testing. Built on the rVSV platform used in the licensed Zaire ebolavirus vaccine and supported by established manufacturing expertise from Hilleman and MSD, this vaccine candidate could become an important tool for Bundibugyo outbreak control and response." Dr Richard Hatchett CEO Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations (CEPI) Hilleman Laboratories will initially take forward development of the rVSV Bundibugyo vaccine candidate starting material generated by IAVI with CEPI funding, and potentially other CEPI funded rVSV vaccine candidates in the future. Hilleman will leverage know-how on the rVSV platform to develop and finalise the manufacturing process and subsequently produce clinical trial material. MSD will serve as a technical adviser to Hilleman Laboratories by contributing proprietary scientific and manufacturing expertise on the rVSV platform. "Collaborating with CEPI, we’re developing the tools to help fight the Bundibugyo virus. Drawing on the latest vaccine technology and our ongoing development work to update the manufacturing process for the Zaire ebolavirus vaccine, we’re racing to develop a Bundibugyo vaccine and make doses for clinical trials." Dr Raman Rao CEO Hilleman Laboratories Hilleman Laboratories will adapt the updated manufacturing process currently in development for MSD’s WHO pre-qualified Zaire ebolavirus vaccine—which uses the rVSV platform—to accelerate the path to clinical trials for the Bundibugyo candidate. Supported by up to $30 million in CEPI funding announced earlier this year, the updated manufacturing process in development for MSD’s Zaire ebolavirus vaccine aims to increase yields and improve thermostability. If successful, this could potentially reduce the cost of the vaccine and enable refrigerated storage for several months, making it easier to deploy in outbreak settings, subject to regulatory review and public health requirements. "Cross-sector collaboration is critical for addressing unmet global health needs and strengthening preparedness—including around Ebola—and we commend CEPI and Hilleman Laboratories on their efforts to develop a Bundibugyo vaccine candidate. By leveraging each partner’s unique strengths, we are hopeful the world will soon have a new tool to respond quickly and effectively to Bundibugyo outbreaks." Chirfi Guindo MSD Shareholder Executive Leader, Hilleman Laboratories Executive Vice President, Strategic Access, Policy & Communications, MSD "We urgently need to strengthen our toolkit against Bundibugyo. The outbreak is in a region faced with conflict, instability, and strained resources, making a holistic response essential. A new vaccine, alongside other interventions such as enhanced surveillance, community engagement, and the testing of diagnostics and treatments, will be vital. Learning lessons from previous outbreaks and the Zaire ebolavirus vaccine, this is a significant step towards developing an affordable vaccine that will reach the communities who need it most." Charlie Weller Head of Vaccines Wellcome Hilleman Laboratories is part of Singapore’s established biomedical sciences ecosystem, contributing to the country's vaccine research, development and manufacturing, with a focus on outbreak preparedness and response. In May 2026, Singapore pledged US$12 million to support CEPI’s work to transform the world's ability to prevent and respond to epidemic and pandemic threats. news.source_body_en: Hilleman Laboratories, a Singapore-based joint venture between MSD and Wellcome, is developing and producing Bundibugyo ebolavirus vaccine doses for clinical trials, supported by CEPI funding. The Bundibugyo virus outbreak, primarily affecting the Democratic Republic of the Congo, is one of the largest on record, with cases rising at a worrying pace. No vaccine is currently approved against the virus, so efforts are focused on advancing vaccine candidates into testing. The rVSV platform, used in the licensed Zaire ebolavirus vaccine, is being leveraged to accelerate development. If early phase trials succeed, the vaccine technology will be transferred to a large-scale manufacturer to produce additional doses for later-stage trials. This initiative aims to ensure rapid, affordable supply of the vaccine in outbreak-affected countries and low- and middle-income settings, provided regulatory approval is obtained. The collaboration highlights the importance of cross-sector efforts in addressing global health challenges like Bundibugyo outbreaks.
news.content_zh: Hilleman实验室是一家由默克公司(MSD)和惠康基金会(Wellcome)在新加坡共同成立的合资企业,正在开发并生产用于临床试验的邦迪布古埃博拉病毒疫苗剂量,该工作得到了CEPI资金的支持。该邦迪布古病毒暴发主要影响刚果民主共和国,是迄今为止记录的最大规模之一,病例数量正以令人担忧的速度上升。目前尚无针对该病毒的疫苗获批,因此工作重点是推进疫苗候选疫苗进入测试阶段。已获批的扎伊尔埃博拉病毒疫苗所使用的rVSV平台将被用于加速开发。如果早期试验成功,疫苗技术将被转移给大规模生产商,以生产更多剂量用于后期试验。该计划旨在确保在暴发受影响的国家以及低收入和中等收入地区,能够快速、经济地提供疫苗,前提是获得监管批准。此次合作凸显了应对全球健康挑战如邦迪布古暴发时跨行业努力的重要性。

Disease Outbreak News Ebola disease caused by Bundibugyo virus - Democratic Republic of the Congo 25 September 2026 See all DONs related to this event Read more about Ebola disease Situation at a glance Since the last Disease Outbreak News was published on 11 September 2026, the Bundibugyo virus outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has expanded further, with two additional health zones affected. These include Bulu health zone in a new province, Sud Ubangi, located on the north-west part of the country and Dungu health zone in Haut-Uélé province, bordering South Sudan. This brings the total number of affected health zones to 63 across seven provinces out of 26 provinces of the country: Bas-Uélé, Haut-Uélé, Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Sud Ubangi and Tshopo. This latest geographic expansion increases the risk of cross-border transmission. As of 23 September 2026, the Democratic Republic of the Congo has reported 7890 confirmed cases, including 3799 deaths, resulting in a crude case fatality ratio (CFR) of 48.1%. At the national level, the number of new cases reported each day remains high. However, the situation varies across the country, with some provinces and health zones experiencing much higher levels of transmission than others. The continuously high CFR, and especially the continuous high rate of deaths occurring in communities, highlights the seriousness of the disease and the persistent challenges in timely case detection and access to early and adequate patient care. These delays can contribute to preventable illness and deaths among people in affected and newly affected areas, while also allowing transmission to continue within households, communities, and healthcare settings. Description of the situation Since the previous Disease Outbreak News was published on 11 September 2026, an additional 1133 confirmed cases, including 532 confirmed deaths, have been reported in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The seven-day moving average shows a resurgence in early September followed by a decline over the most recent reporting days. However, the aggregate national trend conceals substantial variation in transmission intensity across affected provinces and health zones. As of 23 September, the Democratic Republic of the Congo has reported a total of 7890 confirmed cases, including 3799 deaths (CFR 48.1%). A total of 1966 patients have recovered to date. Confirmed cases have been reported from 63 health zones across seven provinces, with 48 health zones from six provinces reporting at least one case in the last 21 days. Ituri remains the most affected province, with 28 of its 36 health zones reporting cases, followed by North Kivu (16/34), Tshopo (7/23), Haut-Uélé (7/13), Bas-Uélé (3/11), South Kivu (1/34), and Sud Ubangi (1/16). No new cases have been reported from South Kivu province since 29 May 2026. Dungu Health Zone in Haut-Uélé province and Bulu in Sud Ubangi are the most recently affected areas. As of 23 September, 70 new confirmed cases had been reported in the preceding 24 hours from 26 health zones located in Ituri, North Kivu, Haut-Uélé, Bas Uélé and Tshopo provinces. Figure 1. Distribution of cumulative confirmed cases of Bundibugyo virus disease in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, as of 23 September Ituri continues to be the epicentre of the outbreak, accounting for 6032 confirmed cases since the start of the outbreak, including 868 new confirmed cases reported in the previous 21 days, as of 23 September. North Kivu is the second most affected province, with a cumulative number of 1480 confirmed cases, including 567 reported in the last 21 days, as of 23 September. North Kivu province continues to report the highest CFR (59.7%) observed in this outbreak; and investigations are ongoing to better understand the factors contributing to this elevated mortality rate. In Ituri, case incidence continues to decline gradually from the peak observed in mid-August, although transmission remains at elevated levels. North Kivu, in contrast, has experienced a substantial increase in incidence, reaching its highest reported level in mid-September, followed by a decline in recent reporting days. Haut-Uélé continues to demonstrate sustained transmission, albeit at levels below the peak recorded in late August, while Tshopo is showing renewed transmission activity following a period of low incidence. In Bas-Uélé, transmission remains sporadic, whereas no recent evidence of transmission has been reported in Sud-Kivu. Sud Ubangi is the seventh province to report a confirmed case of BVD, with one case that was reported on 10 September (Figure 2). The number of individuals requiring follow-up as contact has also risen considerably with the expansion of the outbreak. As of 23 September, 83.4% of identified contacts were successfully monitored during the previous 24 hours with 26 980 contacts seen out of 32 342 requiring follow up. The large volume of contacts under surveillance highlights the extent of potential exposure within affected communities and the substantial demands placed on response operations. The response is being implemented in a challenging humanitarian environment, where conflict, insecurity, displacement, and limited access to basic services continue to affect outbreak control. These constraints continue to hamper surveillance, case finding, contact tracing, infection prevention and control, and timely access to appropriate care, thereby limiting the overall effectiveness of response activities. Figure 2: Number of confirmed Bundibugyo virus disease cases in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, by date of notification, as of 23 September 2026 Figure 3: Number of deaths among confirmed Bundibugyo virus disease cases in the Democratic Republic of the Congo by date of notification, as of 23 September 2026. Epidemiology Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) is a severe Ebola disease caused by the Bundibugyo virus, one of the Orthoebolavirus species. It is a zoonotic disease, with fruit bats suspected to be the natural reservoir. Human infection is thought to occur through close contact with the blood or secretions of infected wildlife, such as bats or non-human primates, and it subsequently spreads from person-to-person through direct contact with the blood, secretions, organs, or other bodily fluids of infected individuals or contaminated surfaces and materials. Transmission is particularly amplified in health-care settings when IPC measures are inadequate and during unsafe burial practices involving direct contact with deceased individuals. The incubation period for BVD ranges from two to 21 days, and infected individuals are not infectious until symptom onset. Early symptoms such as fever, fatigue, muscle pain, headache, and sore throat are non-specific, which complicates clinical diagnosis and can delay detection. These symptoms then progress to gastrointestinal symptoms, organ dysfunction, and, in some cases, haemorrhagic manifestations. The historical CFR from the past two BVD outbreaks, reported in Uganda and in the Democratic Republic of the Congo in 2007 and 2012, were 30% and 50%, respectively. Differentiating BVD from other endemic febrile illnesses such as malaria is challenging without laboratory confirmation using polymerase chain reaction (PCR) or antigen- or antibody-based assays. Outbreak control relies on rapid case identification, isolation and care, contact tracing, safe burials and strong community engagement, as no approved vaccines or specific treatments currently exist for BVD. Since first detected in May 2026, this BVD outbreak has rapidly evolved into a large and geographically expanding epidemic in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, with sustained transmission, high mortality and an increasing risk of further international spread. The current outbreak is the second documented Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak in the country, after the 2012 outbreak, and the largest Ebola disease outbreak ever recorded in the Democratic Republic of the Congo irrespective of Ebola virus species. The population at greatest risk of exposure is concentrated in communities living in and moving through the health areas with active transmission. Disease Outbreak News Ebola disease caused by Bundibugyo virus - Democratic Republic of the Congo 25 September 2026 See all DONs related to this event Read more about Ebola disease Situation at a glance Since the last Disease Outbreak News was published on 11 September 2026, the Bundibugyo virus outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has expanded further, with two additional health zones affected. These include Bulu health zone in a new province, Sud Ubangi, located on the north-west part of the country and Dungu health zone in Haut-Uélé province, bordering South Sudan. This brings the total number of affected health zones to 63 across seven provinces out of 26 provinces of the country: Bas-Uélé, Haut-Uélé, Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Sud Ubangi and Tshopo. This latest geographic expansion increases the risk of cross-border transmission. As of 23 September 2026, the Democratic Republic of the Congo has reported 7890 confirmed cases, including 3799 deaths, resulting in a crude case fatality ratio (CFR) of 48.1%. At the national level, the number of new cases reported each day remains high. However, the situation varies across the country, with some provinces and health zones experiencing much higher levels of transmission than others. The continuously high CFR, and especially the continuous high rate of deaths occurring in communities, highlights the seriousness of the disease and the persistent challenges in timely case detection and access to early and adequate patient care. These delays can contribute to preventable illness and deaths among people in affected and newly affected areas, while also allowing transmission to continue within households, communities, and healthcare settings. Description of the situation Since the previous Disease Outbreak News was published on 11 September 2026, an additional 1133 confirmed cases, including 532 confirmed deaths, have been reported in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The seven-day moving average shows a resurgence in early September followed by a decline over the most recent reporting days. However, the aggregate national trend conceals substantial variation in transmission intensity across affected provinces and health zones. As of 23 September, the Democratic Republic of the Congo has reported a total of 7890 confirmed cases, including 3799 deaths (CFR 48.1%). A total of 1966 patients have recovered to date. Confirmed cases have been reported from 63 health zones across seven provinces, with 48 health zones from six provinces reporting at least one case in the last 21 days. Ituri remains the most affected province, with 28 of its 36 health zones reporting cases, followed by North Kivu (16/34), Tshopo (7/23), Haut-Uélé (7/13), Bas-Uélé (3/11), South Kivu (1/34), and Sud Ubangi (1/16). No new cases have been reported from South Kivu province since 29 May 2026. Dungu Health Zone in Haut-Uélé province and Bulu in Sud Ubangi are the most recently affected areas. As of 23 September, 70 new confirmed cases had been reported in the preceding 24 hours from 26 health zones located in Ituri, North Kivu, Haut-Uélé, Bas Uélé and Tshopo provinces. Figure 1. Distribution of cumulative confirmed cases of Bundibugyo virus disease in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, as of 23 September Ituri continues to be the epicentre of the outbreak, accounting for 6032 confirmed cases since the start of the outbreak, including 868 new confirmed cases reported in the previous 21 days, as of 23 September. North Kivu is the second most affected province, with a cumulative number of 1480 confirmed cases, including 567 reported in the last 21 days, as of 23 September. North Kivu province continues to report the highest CFR (59.7%) observed in this outbreak; and investigations are ongoing to better understand the factors contributing to this elevated mortality rate. In Ituri, case incidence continues to decline gradually from the peak observed in mid-August, although transmission remains at elevated levels. North Kivu, in contrast, has experienced a substantial increase in incidence, reaching its highest reported level in mid-September, followed by a decline in recent reporting days. Haut-Uélé continues to demonstrate sustained transmission, albeit at levels below the peak recorded in late August, while Tshopo is showing renewed transmission activity following a period of low incidence. In Bas-Uélé, transmission remains sporadic, whereas no recent evidence of transmission has been reported in Sud-Kivu. Sud Ubangi is the seventh province to report a confirmed case of BVD, with one case that was reported on 10 September (Figure 2). The number of individuals requiring follow-up as contact has also risen considerably with the expansion of the outbreak. As of 23 September, 83.4% of identified contacts were successfully monitored during the previous 24 hours with 26 980 contacts seen out of 32 342 requiring follow up. The large volume of contacts under surveillance highlights the extent of potential exposure within affected communities and the substantial demands placed on response operations. The response is being implemented in a challenging humanitarian environment, where conflict, insecurity, displacement, and limited access to basic services continue to affect outbreak control. These constraints continue to hamper surveillance, case finding, contact tracing, infection prevention and control, and timely access to appropriate care, thereby limiting the overall effectiveness of response activities. Epidemiology Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) is a severe Ebola disease caused by the Bundibugyo virus, one of the Orthoebolavirus species. It is a zoonotic disease, with fruit bats suspected to be the natural reservoir. Human infection is thought to occur through close contact with the blood or secretions of infected wildlife, such as bats or non-human primates, and it subsequently spreads from person-to-person through direct contact with the blood, secretions, organs, or other bodily fluids of infected individuals or contaminated surfaces and materials. Transmission is particularly amplified in health-care settings when IPC measures are inadequate and during unsafe burial practices involving direct contact with deceased individuals. The incubation period for BVD ranges from two to 21 days, and infected individuals are not infectious until symptom onset. Early symptoms such as fever, fatigue, muscle pain, headache, and sore throat are non-specific, which complicates clinical diagnosis and can delay detection. These symptoms then progress to gastrointestinal symptoms, organ dysfunction, and, in some cases, haemorrhagic manifestations. The historical CFR from the past two BVD outbreaks, reported in Uganda and in the Democratic Republic of the Congo in 2007 and 2012, were 30% and 50%, respectively. Differentiating BVD from other endemic febrile illnesses such as malaria is challenging without laboratory confirmation using polymerase chain reaction (PCR) or antigen- or antibody-based assays. Outbreak control relies on rapid case identification, isolation and care, contact tracing, safe burials and strong community engagement, as no approved vaccines or specific treatments currently exist for BVD. Since first detected in May 2026, this BVD outbreak has rapidly evolved into a large and geographically expanding epidemic in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, with sustained transmission, high mortality and an increasing risk of further international spread. The current outbreak is the second documented Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak in the country, after the 2012 outbreak, and the largest Ebola disease outbreak ever recorded in the Democratic Republic of the Congo irrespective of Ebola virus species. The population at greatest risk of exposure is concentrated in communities living in and moving through the health areas with active transmission. A substantial scale-up is ongoing across all response pillars to get ahead of the outbreak. WHO risk assessment On 14 August 2026, WHO reassessed the risk of the outbreak of BVD, incorporating newly available information on the evolving situation. The risk for countries sharing land borders with the Democratic Republic of the Congo was separated from the risk for other countries in the African Region. The risk in the Democratic Republic of the Congo was assessed as very high, the risk for countries sharing land borders with the Democratic Republic of the Congo was assessed as high, and the risks for the rest of the African region and at the global level was again assessed as low. Search|t Updates Countries Disasters Organizations Topics Jobs Training Informing humanitarians worldwide 24/7 — a service provided by UN OCHA DR Congo + 1 more Ebola Bundibugyo Virus Disease Outbreak Democratic Republic of the Congo | Uganda Weekly External Situation Report 19, Data as of 20 September 2026 Format Situation Report Source WHO Posted 24 Sep 2026 Originally published 24 Sep 2026 Origin View original Attachments Download Report (PDF | 1.44 MB) Event description The Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has expanded further, with Dungu Health Zone in Haut-Uélé Province, bordering South Sudan, being the latest affected, bringing the total number of health zones affected to 63 since the start of the outbreak. This latest geographic expansion heightens concern about further spread towards international borders, while transmission within the country remains increasingly heterogeneous across affected provinces and health zones. Since External Situation Report #18, a further 475 confirmed cases and 222 confirmed deaths have been reported, bringing the cumulative total to 7733 confirmed cases, including 3732 deaths [crude case fatality ratio (CFR 48.3%)], as of 20 September 2026. Ituri remains the principal focus, although its relative contribution continues to decline, accounting for 76.9% of cumulative confirmed cases, while substantial transmission continues in Nord-Kivu and persists in Haut-Uélé. At the national level, daily incidence remains high and fluctuating, with the seven-day moving average rebounding in early September before declining in the most recent days. This national pattern masks divergent provincial trajectories. Ituri continues a gradual decline from its late-July peak but remains at a high level, while Nord-Kivu experienced a marked increase, reaching its highest incidence in mid-September, followed by an apparent decline in recent days. Transmission in Haut-Uélé remains sustained but below its August peak, while Tshopo shows renewed activity from a low baseline. Bas-Uélé continues to report sporadic transmission, with no recent transmission evident in Sud-Kivu. Overall, the epidemic remains geographically heterogeneous, with recent declines in the principal transmission areas occurring alongside persistent low-level transmission and continued geographic expansion to new areas. news.content: Skip to main content Help Log in ReliefWeb Search Content Search What are you looking for? Search|t Updates Countries Disasters Organizations Topics Jobs Training Informing humanitarians worldwide 24/7 — a service provided by UN OCHA DR Congo UNICEF Democratic Republic of the Congo Humanitarian Situation Report No. 3 – Ebola Outbreak (Bundibugyo Virus), 31 August Format Situation Report Source UNICEF Posted 25 Sep 2026 Originally published 24 Sep 2026 Attachments Download Report (PDF | 1.54 MB) Highlights UNICEF is scaling up its response from 49 to 60 affected and high-risk health zones, supporting Government-led efforts across community-based surveillance, RCCE, IPC/WASH, nutrition, MHPSS, clinical care, PSEA and continuity of essential services. In August, 11,723 community actors, including 6,546 community mobilizers (RECOs), were trained and mobilized on RCCE and community-based surveillance. Since the beginning of the response, a total of 24,750 frontline workers, including 12,555 community mobilizers (RECOs), have been mobilized. UNICEF-supported community surveillance networks generated 29,689 alerts in August, representing an 186 per cent increase from the previous reporting period. Contact tracing coverage reached 88 per cent, with 22,499 of 25,560 contacts followed, strengthening outbreak detection and monitoring efforts. UNICEF and partners continued to deliver lifesaving support despite operational constraints due to the Ebola outbreak. In August, 126,078 people were reached with essential supplies and emergency health and nutrition assistance through the rapid response mechanism. Ahead of the new school year, UNICEF and the Ministry of Education agreed on measures to ensure the safe reopening of schools in Ebola-affected provinces. UNICEF provided technical support to establish reopening standards based on risk assessments of the BVD spread in schools and will support 900 schools with WASH and IPC supplies, MHPSS services, and community awareness activities on Ebola prevention. UNICEF requires US$113.5 million for its revised six-month response plan. As of 31 August 2026, US$34.4 million had been mobilized, leaving a US$79 million funding gap, equivalent to 70 per cent of the requirement. EPIDEMIOLOGICAL SITUATION UPDATE Between 1 and 31 August 2026, the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) reported 2,581 confirmed Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) cases and 1,420 deaths. As of 31 August, cumulative confirmed cases had reached 6,186, including 3,007 deaths, corresponding to a case fatality ratio (CFR) of 48.6%. The outbreak continued to expand geographically with confirmed cases reported for the first time in Bas-Uélé Province, bringing the number of affected provinces to six (Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Haut-Uélé, Tshopo and Bas-Uélé). During August, an additional 12 health zones reported confirmed cases, increasing the total to 60 affected health zones, representing 39.7 per cent of the country's 151 health zones. The outbreak is now the largest Ebola outbreak ever recorded in the DRC and the second largest globally. Ituri Province remains the epicentre, accounting for 81.9 per cent of all confirmed cases (5,065) and 2,305 deaths followed by North Kivu (868 cases, 589 deaths) and Haut-Uélé (227 cases, 100 deaths). Transmission also continued in Tshopo, South Kivu and Bas-Uélé. Women and girls represent 53 per cent of reported cases. Children under 17 account for approximately 30.2 per cent of cases and 21.8 per cent of reported deaths, with children under five bearing the greatest burden, representing nearly two-thirds of deaths among children under 18. During August, 42 health workers were affected, underscoring ongoing risks to frontline responders. The report also mentions measures to ensure the safe reopening of schools in affected provinces. UNICEF requires US$113.5 million for its revised six-month response plan, with US$34.4 million mobilized as of 31 August, leaving a US$79 million funding gap.

analysis_zh.time: 该报告于2026年9月25日发布,事件日期为2026年8月31日。2026年8月期间,暴发继续向地理上扩展。
analysis_zh.location_and_population: 刚果民主共和国(DRC),具体包括Ituri、North Kivu、South Kivu、Haut-Uélé、Tshopo和Bas-Uélé省份。女性和女孩占报告病例的53%,17岁以下儿童占病例的约30.2%和死亡的21.8%。
analysis_zh.event: 在刚果民主共和国报告了一起由邦巴比古病毒引起的埃博拉 暴发。联合国儿童基金会和刚果民主共和国政府正在扩大其响应努力,包括基于社区的 监测 和对基本服务的支持。
analysis_zh.scale_impact_and_risk: 截至2026年8月31日,刚果民主共和国报告了2,581例确诊病例和1,420例死亡,由邦巴比古病毒引起。累计确诊病例达到6,186例,死亡人数为3,007例,病死率为48.6%。暴发在六个省份扩展,2026年8月期间有42名医护人员受到影响。
analysis_zh.response_status_and_uncertainty: UNICEF is supporting Government-led efforts in community-based surveillance, RCCE, IPC/WASH, nutrition, MHPSS, clinical care, and ensuring the continuity of essential services. Contact tracing coverage reached 88%, and 126,078 people were reached with essential supplies and emergency health and nutrition assistance in August 2026. A funding gap of US$79 million remains.

To date, no cases of Ebola disease have been confirmed in the United States because of this outbreak. The overall risk to the American public and travelers remains low. Outbreak overview Risk to the United States To date, no Ebola cases associated with this outbreak have been reported in the United States. The likelihood of Ebola spreading to the United States is considered very low. If a case was diagnosed in the United States, the risk of Ebola spreading in the United States is also low due to the strength of our public health system and infection control measures. CDC is responding to an outbreak of Ebola in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). This outbreak is spreading substantially faster than previous Ebola outbreaks and is now the second-largest Ebola outbreak on record. The outbreak is caused by Bundibugyo virus, a type of Ebola virus. In DRC, cases have been confirmed in Bas-Uele, Haut-Uele, Ituri, Nord-Kivu (North Kivu), Sud-Kivu (South Kivu), Sud-Ubangi (South Ubangi), and Tshopo provinces. This is the 17th outbreak of Ebola in DRC. This Ebola outbreak surpassed 1,000 confirmed cases within 40 days of response activation. In comparison, the 2018 Ebola outbreak in DRC took approximately 235 days to reach more than 1,000 cases. South Kivu has reported no confirmed cases since May 29. Uganda also reported cases of Ebola at the same time DRC declared an outbreak. Uganda reported 21 confirmed and probable cases and 3 deaths. The last reported case there was confirmed June 21. Response challenges The response to this outbreak is challenging due to a number of complex circumstances in the region. Limited health infrastructure, including limited access to healthcare, diagnostic and laboratory services, infection prevention and control supplies, and other basic services make stopping this outbreak more difficult. Ongoing conflict in the area where the outbreak is occurring creates security issues and complicates contact tracing and infection prevention and control. Violence against healthcare workers and shortages of personal protective equipment are leading to healthcare workers becoming infected while treating patients. Frequent population movement and cross-border travel increase the risk of spread to Uganda, South Sudan, Rwanda, and to other areas. Lack of trust in the government and misinformation make communicating about Ebola more difficult. To reduce the risk of Ebola importation into the United States, U.S. entry for travelers who were recently in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is temporarily restricted. Travelers, including Americans, who have been in DRC within 21 days of their flight will not be allowed to board commercial flights with U.S. destinations. All U.S. citizens and U.S. nationals who have been in DRC should plan to remain outside DRC for 21 days before entering the United States. This includes all passengers with an intermediate stop in DRC or on multi-stop itineraries via DRC regardless of whether they disembark or stay on the airplane. U.S. citizens and U.S. nationals who have been present in Uganda or South Sudan (and not present in DRC) within 21 days of arrival in the United States must only enter through designated airports for enhanced screening. This process is in addition to CDC's Order, under 42 CFR 71.40, that continued the temporary entry restrictions to the United States for certain categories of travelers after they were in DRC, Uganda, or South Sudan. CDC recommends avoiding all travel to Ituri and Nord-Kivu (North Kivu) provinces and avoiding nonessential travel to Haut-Uele and Tshopo provinces in DRC. Travelers to other parts of DRC or Uganda should take enhanced precautions to avoid Ebola exposure and monitor for symptoms while traveling and for 21 days after leaving. Latest data Reported cases This is a rapidly evolving situation, and case counts are subject to change. Suspected cases and suspected deaths in DRC have been temporarily excluded from the count pending ongoing investigations and data standardization. The Uganda MoH does not include suspected cases in their official reporting. Map of affected areas View LargerDownload To date, the Ebola disease outbreak in DRC has been confirmed in Bas-Uele, Haut-Uele, Ituri, Nord-Kivu (North Kivu), Sud-Kivu (South Kivu), Sud-Ubangi (South Ubangi), and Tshopo provinces. Cases related to the DRC outbreak also have been reported in Uganda's capital of Kampala. CDC response CDC is working internationally and domestically to respond to this outbreak and prevent Ebola from entering the United States. About 500 people at CDC are involved in responding to the outbreak, including more than 120 people deployed to the affected countries. To date, no cases of Ebola disease have been confirmed in the United States because of this outbreak. The overall risk to the American public and travelers remains low. Outbreak overview Risk to the United States To date, no Ebola cases associated with this outbreak have been reported in the United States. The likelihood of Ebola spreading to the United States is considered very low. If a case was diagnosed in the United States, the risk of Ebola spreading in the United States is also low due to the strength of our public health system and infection control measures. CDC is responding to an outbreak of Ebola in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). This outbreak is spreading substantially faster than previous Ebola outbreaks and is now the second-largest Ebola outbreak on record. The outbreak is caused by Bundibugyo virus, a type of Ebola virus. In DRC, cases have been confirmed in Bas-Uele, Haut-Uele, Ituri, Nord-Kivu (North Kivu), Sud-Kivu (South Kivu), Sud-Ubangi (South Ubangi), and Tshopo provinces. This is the 17th outbreak of Ebola in DRC. This Ebola outbreak surpassed 1,000 confirmed cases within 40 days of response activation. In comparison, the 2018 Ebola outbreak in DRC took approximately 235 days to reach more than 1,000 cases. South Kivu has reported no confirmed cases since May 29. Uganda also reported cases of Ebola at the same time DRC declared an outbreak. Uganda reported 21 confirmed and probable cases and 3 deaths. The last reported case there was confirmed June 21. Response challenges The response to this outbreak is challenging due to a number of complex circumstances in the region. Limited health infrastructure, including limited access to healthcare, diagnostic and laboratory services, infection prevention and control supplies, and other basic services make stopping this outbreak more difficult. Ongoing conflict in the area where the outbreak is occurring creates security issues and complicates contact tracing and infection prevention and control. Violence against healthcare workers and shortages of personal protective equipment are leading to healthcare workers becoming infected while treating patients. Frequent population movement and cross-border travel increase the risk of spread to Uganda, South Sudan, Rwanda, and to other areas. Lack of trust in the government and misinformation make communicating about Ebola more difficult. To reduce the risk of Ebola importation into the United States, U.S. entry for travelers who were recently in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is temporarily restricted. Travelers, including Americans, who have been in DRC within 21 days of their flight will not be allowed to board commercial flights with U.S. destinations. All U.S. citizens and U.S. nationals who have been in DRC should plan to remain outside DRC for 21 days before entering the United States. This includes all passengers with an intermediate stop in DRC or on multi-stop itineraries via DRC regardless of whether they disembark or stay on the airplane. U.S. citizens and U.S. nationals who have been present in Uganda or South Sudan (and not present in DRC) within 21 days of arrival in the United States must only enter through designated airports for enhanced screening. This process is in addition to CDC's Order, under 42 CFR 71.40, that continued the temporary entry restrictions to the United States for certain categories of travelers after they were in DRC, Uganda, or South Sudan. CDC recommends avoiding all travel to Ituri and Nord-Kivu (North Kivu) provinces and avoiding nonessential travel to Haut-Uele and Tshopo provinces in DRC. Travelers to other parts of DRC or Uganda should take enhanced precautions to avoid Ebola exposure and monitor for symptoms while traveling and for 21 days after leaving. Cases related to the DRC outbreak also have been reported in Uganda's capital of Kampala. CDC response CDC is working internationally and domestically to respond to this outbreak and prevent Ebola from entering the United States. About 500 people at CDC are involved in responding to the outbreak, including more than 120 people deployed to the affected countries. news.content_title: An approved Ebola antibody may miss its mark against Bundibugyo virus
news.content: Antibodies developed for one Ebola virus species face a different viral target in the 2026 outbreak. Structural models reveal why testing each treatment against Bundibugyo virus matters. Study: Early insights into predicted efficacy of Ebola monoclonal antibodies for the 2026 Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak . Image Credit: Corona Borealis Studio / Shutterstock In a recent study published in the journal Nature Communications , researchers modeled the binding behavior of approved and experimental Ebola monoclonal antibodies ( mAbs ) against the virus causing the emerging 2026 Bundibugyo virus disease ( BVD ) outbreak. The research team first gathered 44 Bundibugyo virus ( BDBV ) genomes collected in 2007, 2012, and 2026, including 12 from the 2026 outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo ( DRC ) and Uganda. They then identified mutations in these sequences and used structural modeling to map changes in the viral glycoprotein ( GP ) and to computationally predict each mAb's binding stability. The authors also checked whether the identified mutations persisted in additional available sequences. The modeling predicted that the licensed monotherapy mAb114 (Ebanga) would exhibit displaced binding and a sharply reduced affinity for BDBV, an observation the researchers attributed to key epitope mutations. For Inmazeb, while two individual components of the triple-antibody cocktail were predicted to miss their intended sites on their own, the model predicted that the three antibodies bound at their intended sites together. The most notable finding was that both components of the experimental pan-ebolavirus cocktail MBP134 targeted entirely conserved epitopes and were predicted to bind without structural displacement. Together, these computational predictions indicate that therapeutic efficacy cannot be assumed when moving across divergent viral species, offering evidence to help prioritize experimental testing and guide outbreak response in the DRC and Uganda. Background Ebolavirus outbreaks carry devastating health consequences, with fatality rates reaching as high as 90% in some past outbreaks. Treatments currently approved by the United States Food and Drug Administration ( FDA ; specifically, mAb114 and REGN-EB3 [Inmazeb]) were developed for Ebola virus ( EBOV , Orthoebolavirus zairense ). The 2026 outbreak in Central and East Africa is driven by Bundibugyo virus (BDBV, Orthoebolavirus bundibugyoense ), which is itself an orthoebolavirus. Genetic analyses have demonstrated that O. zairense and O. bundibugyoense share only 63.9% genome-wide identity and roughly 65% amino acid similarity in their glycoprotein composition. The international health community has therefore faced uncertainty about whether approved EBOV therapeutics could neutralize BDBV or whether the substantial genetic divergence between the two species might limit their effectiveness. About the study To address these knowledge gaps, the authors analyzed 44 BDBV whole-genome sequences spanning 2007, 2012, and 2026, including 12 collected from the 2026 outbreak (eight from the DRC and four from Uganda). The researchers checked whether identified mutations persisted in additional available sequences. The study investigated predictions for three primary therapeutic candidates: 1. mAb114 (commercially named 'Ebanga'), 2. Inmazeb (a trimeric cocktail composed of Atoltivimab, Odesivimab, and Maftivimab), and 3. An experimental cocktail called MBP134 (synthesized by combining ADI-15878 and ADI-15946). The computational work used AlphaFold 3 ( AF3 ) deep-learning structural predictions plus Rosetta-based in silico mutagenesis to quantify changes in binding free energy (ΔΔG in kilocalories per mole [ kcal/mol ]). The predictions were further used to compute how tightly antibody surfaces packed against the viral protein and the steric impact of site-specific glycosylation at Asn563. Study findings Structural analyses found that BDBV has evolved 10 shared glycoprotein substitutions in the 2012 and 2026 sequences relative to the 2007 reference. Two novel mutations, Y387H and R506S, were present in all 12 analyzed 2026 sequences and absent from the earlier sequences compared. Antibody binding predictions showed that, for mAb114, the critical recognition region (residues 111–119) harbored E112D and P116A mutations, which the model indicated would cause the antibody to dock off-target. Subsequent mutagenesis simulations estimated that E112D destabilized the interface. P116A was estimated to reduce docking affinity. The simulations indicated that, when modeled as monotherapies, two of Inmazeb's components, Atoltivimab and Maftivimab, would fail to engage their intended epitopes. The third component, Odesivimab, was predicted to bind its intended site independently. Maftivimab alone was predicted to be severely disrupted by natural glycan shielding at Asn563. When the three antibodies were modeled together, the structural prediction showed glycan accommodation and binding at the intended sites. Modeling also showed that both components of MBP134 (ADI-15878 and ADI-15946) targeted epitopes that remained 100% conserved in all 44 BDBV genomes and were predicted to bind at their intended target sites without structural displacement. Conclusions The findings suggest that epitope conservation and interactions among cocktail components may influence binding. The authors note that their static computational models cannot capture the dynamic physiological movements of the viral glycoprotein or the full complexity of real-world antibody binding, and they caution that these findings should not be used alone to alter clinical practice. The predictions provide a rationale for comparing Maftivimab with the complete Inmazeb cocktail through experimental testing. These computational findings need urgent validation through binding measurements and live-virus or pseudovirus neutralization assays. The results identify MBP134 and the full Inmazeb cocktail as candidates for experimental evaluation; their effectiveness against BDBV remains unknown. Journal reference: Nabukeera, K. C., et al. (2026). Early insights into predicted efficacy of Ebola monoclonal antibodies for the 2026 Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak. Nature Communications . DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-78077-9. https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-026-78077-9

The simulations indicated that, when modeled as monotherapies, two of Inmazeb's components, Atoltivimab and Maftivimab, would fail to engage their intended epitopes. The third component, Odesivimab, was predicted to bind its intended site independently. Maftivimab alone was predicted to be severely disrupted by natural glycan shielding at Asn563. When the three antibodies were modeled together, the structural prediction showed glycan accommodation and binding at the intended sites. Modeling also showed that both components of MBP134 (ADI-15878 and ADI-15946) targeted epitopes that remained 100% conserved in all 44 BDBV genomes and were predicted to bind at their intended target sites without structural displacement. Conclusions The findings suggest that epitope conservation and interactions among cocktail components may influence binding. The authors note that their static computational models cannot capture the dynamic physiological movements of the viral glycoprotein or the full complexity of real-world antibody binding, and they caution that these findings should not be used alone to alter clinical practice. The predictions provide a rationale for comparing Maftivimab with the complete Inmazeb cocktail through experimental testing. These computational findings need urgent validation through binding measurements and live-virus or pseudovirus neutralization assays. The results identify MBP134 and the full Inmazeb cocktail as candidates for experimental evaluation; their effectiveness against BDBV remains unknown. Journal reference: Nabukeera, K. C., et al. analysis.brief_en: A recent study published in Nature Communications investigated the efficacy of approved and experimental Ebola monoclonal antibodies against the Bundibugyo virus (BDBV) during the 2026 outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and Uganda. Researchers analyzed 44 BDBV genomes, including 12 from the 2026 outbreak, and identified key mutations that may affect antibody binding. The study found that the licensed monoclonal antibody mAb114 (Ebanga) would exhibit displaced binding and reduced affinity for BDBV due to epitope mutations. Inmazeb, a triple-antibody cocktail, showed mixed results, with two components failing to bind their intended sites when used as monotherapies but potentially working together. The experimental cocktail MBP134 was predicted to bind effectively due to targeting conserved epitopes. However, the authors emphasized that these computational findings require validation through experimental testing, as they cannot fully capture the dynamic nature of antibody-virus interactions. The study highlights the importance of tailoring treatments to specific viral strains, especially in the context of the 2026 BDBV outbreak, and underscores the need for further research to guide clinical responses in the DRC and Uganda.

news.title_zh: 一种获批的埃博拉抗体可能对邦迪布古病毒无效

news.content_zh: 一项最近发表在《自然·通讯》上的研究调查了获批和实验性的埃博拉单克隆抗体在2026年暴发期间对刚果民主共和国(DRC)和乌干达的邦迪布古病毒(BDBV)的疗效。研究人员分析了44例BDBV 基因组,其中包括12例来自2026年暴发的样本,并确定了可能影响抗体结合的关键突变。研究发现,获批的单克隆抗体mAb114(Ebanga)由于表位突变的变化,可能对BDBV表现出位移结合和亲和力降低。Inmazeb是一种三抗体联合疗法,其结果显示混合效果,其中两个组分在作为单药使用时未能结合其目标位点,但可能在联合使用时有效。实验性联合疗法MBP134被预测能够有效结合BDBV,因为它针对的是保守的表位。然而,作者强调这些计算结果需要通过实验验证,因为它们无法完全反映抗体与病毒相互作用的动态特性。该研究突出了针对特定病毒株定制治疗的重要性,尤其是在2026年BDBV 暴发的背景下,并强调了需要进一步研究以指导刚果民主共和国和乌干达的临床应对措施。

Visit our Support pages Trending / Diagnostics & Laboratory Medicine / Researchers Face Challenges Controlling Bundibugyo Virus Outbreak SEP 24, 2026 5:40 AM PDT Share Researchers Face Challenges Controlling Bundibugyo Virus Outbreak WRITTEN BY: Ashley Pearson The Democratic Republic of the Congo is currently experiencing a Bundibugyo virus (BDBV) outbreak. BDBV can cause severe hemmorhagic disease. Currently, no specific licensed vaccine exists for the treatment or prevention of BDBV. However, early supportive care and early detection can improve survival. Before 2026, no validated test existed to diagnose BDBV. Although BDBV is closely related to ebolavirus as a distinct species within the genus Orthebolavirus, standard older rapid tests designed for Zaire ebolavirus do not cross-detect BDBV. The BDBV outbreak highlighted ongoing challenges European public research institutions and diagnostic companies face in regulatory evaluation of diagnostic tests. After the COVID-19 pandemic, the European Union tightened regulations for new diagnostics, requiring each test to undergo its own validation study. If conducted outside a network of laboratories, validation studies can take months or years to complete. However, when labortatories across Euriope can collaborate, tests can undergo comprehensive analytical and clinical assessment in weeks. An international network of nine laboratories, including members of the German Center for Infection Research (DZIF), the German National University Medicine Network (NUM), and several European research consortia, encompassing major university hospitals with high-containment BSL-4 (Biosafety Level 4, the highest and most stringent level of biological safety containment used in research laboratories) facilities, was able to evaluaute four candidate PCR tests from two manufacturerers thoroughly within two weeks. The comprehensive analytical and clinical assessment showed no evidence of cross-reactivity. The World Health Organization (WHO) granted its first Emergency Use Listing (EUL) to one of the PCR tests studied to accelerate outbreak response. Additionally, a BDBV vaccine is in development. Scientists at DZIF are investigating whether vaccination against Ebola virus could generate antibodies that neutralize BDBV. The Ebola vaccine is readily available to public health officials to distribute in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Moreover, the Ebola vaccine has been validated through comprehensive analytical and clinical assessment for many years. Although findings suggest that the licensed Ebola vaccine may provide some cross-protection against BDBV in studies using non-human primates and small volunteer groups, more research is needed to confirm the vaccine's efficacy. Source: EurekAlert Picture source: Pixabay Share About the Author Ashley Pearson Master's (MA/MS/Other) Ashley (she/her) is a scientific writer. Her writing has been featured on Labroots, Public Health Policy Reviews, and the Pharmacy Times, among other outlets. She received her B.S. in Biology and Creative Writing from Knox College and her M.S. in Biological Sciences from Eastern Illinois University. She is currently a full-time PharmD student at Midwestern University and is expected to graduate May 2028. Infectious Diseases Prof. Yap Boum II, Head of Emergency Preparedness and Response at Africa CDC, disclosed this on Thursday, during a webinar on the ongoing Ebola outbreak in the country. ADVERTISEMENT Boum said the outbreak involved the Bundibugyo virus, a less commonly detected Ebola species, rather than the Zaire strain that has been associated with most previous Ebola outbreaks in the DRC. According to him, diagnostic kits available in eastern DRC initially could not detect the Bundibugyo virus. He said the diagnostic gap allowed the disease to spread for months before laboratory confirmation triggered a full-scale response. Boum said the outbreak was officially detected and declared on May 15, nearly five months after transmission had started in the affected region. Medical Tests & Exams He said the delay contributed to the rapid escalation of the outbreak from just eight cases recorded in three health zones to more than 2,000 cases across 46 health zones. The outbreak has since spread to 63 health zones across seven provinces, according to the Africa CDC official, making it the largest Ebola outbreak recorded in the DRC. Boum identified insecurity and poor access to some communities in eastern DRC as additional obstacles to containing the disease. Discover more Medical Literature & Resources Africans & Diaspora Public Health He said the security situation had hampered active case searches, contact tracing and the ability of response teams to reach affected communities. Community mistrust also complicated containment efforts, he said, forcing health authorities and response partners to intensify community engagement and expand community-based response activities. Read also: NCDC Tightens Surveillance As Ebola Outbreak Spreads In DR Congo Ebola: Enugu Strengthens Preparedness as Mbah, NCDC Intensify Prevention Measures DRC Bans Mass Gatherings In Kinshasa, 3 Other Provinces As Ebola Cases Rise The Africa CDC official said the current outbreak was different from previous Ebola outbreaks in the DRC because of the virus species involved, insecurity, limited accessibility and concerns among affected communities. Biological Sciences He warned that the outbreak highlighted the need for stronger diagnostic preparedness, particularly for less common pathogens that may circulate undetected before laboratory confirmation. Boum called for increased resources and political support to strengthen the response and enable health workers to safely access affected communities. He stressed that controlling the outbreak would require more than financial resources, saying security, community cooperation and access to affected areas were equally critical to stopping transmission. analysis.brief_en: The Africa CDC has identified delayed detection and diagnostic challenges as key factors contributing to the rapid spread of the Ebola virus in the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). The outbreak, which was officially declared on May 15, 2026, involved the Bundibugyo virus, a less common species, rather than the Zaire strain. Initially, diagnostic kits in the region could not detect the Bundibugyo virus, allowing the disease to spread for months before laboratory confirmation. The outbreak escalated from eight cases in three health zones to over 2,000 cases across 46 health zones, and has since spread to 63 health zones across seven provinces, making it the largest recorded in the DRC. Insecurity and poor access to communities further hindered containment efforts, while community mistrust complicated response activities. The Africa CDC called for increased resources, political support, and community engagement to address these challenges and control the outbreak. They emphasized that security, cooperation, and access to affected areas are equally critical to stopping transmission.

news.content_zh: 非洲疾控中心已确认检测延迟和诊断困难是导致刚果民主共和国东部暴发迅速传播的关键因素。该暴发于2026年5月15日被正式宣布,涉及的是较少见的邦迪布古病毒,而非扎伊尔毒株。最初,该地区的诊断试剂盒无法检测到邦迪布古病毒,使得疾病在实验室确认前持续传播数月。暴发从三个卫生区的八例病例迅速上升至46个卫生区的2000多例病例,此后已蔓延至七个省份的63个卫生区,成为刚果民主共和国记录的最大规模疫情。安全局势不佳和社区接触困难进一步阻碍了控制措施的实施,而社区的不信任也使应对活动复杂化。非洲疾控中心呼吁增加资源、政治支持和社区参与,以应对这些挑战并控制暴发。他们强调,安全、合作和对受影响地区的接触同样关键,以阻止传播的传播。
